content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 3: Security Principles, Threats, and Standards. It builds practical understanding of Security Verification and Testing Standards with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Security Verification and Testing Standards gives you the mental model needed to recognize where a security promise begins and ends. Define scope and expected behavior first, combine automated signals with manual verification, record reproducible sanitized evidence, prioritize confirmed risk, and retest the fix.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Security Verification and Testing Standards can be understood through this sequence: Define authorized scope → Form a test hypothesis → Record sanitized evidence → Retest the fix. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 21.1 OWASP ASVS and security verification requirements; 21.2 OWASP WSTG and testing methodology; 21.3 OWASP Cheat Sheet Series; 21.4 NIST Secure Software Development Framework; 21.5 Mapping application risks to testing requirements; 21.6 Using standards as living project checklists. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Define scope and expected behavior first, combine automated signals with manual verification, record reproducible sanitized evidence, prioritize confirmed risk, and retest the fix.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Security Verification and Testing Standards
content_blocks.code:
Topic: Security Verification and Testing Standards
Review artifact: define scope, assumptions, control owner, expected secure behavior, failure behavior, and a reproducible verification step.
content_blocks.expected_output: A written review artifact names the control and the evidence needed to verify it.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local/owned application or explicitly authorized test target. Record only sanitized synthetic evidence; use human review for behavior that a static snippet cannot prove.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Define scope and expected behavior first, combine automated signals with manual verification, record reproducible sanitized evidence, prioritize confirmed risk, and retest the fix. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Security Verification and Testing Standards”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Security Verification and Testing Standards in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Security Verification and Testing Standards is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Define scope and expected behavior first, combine automated signals with manual verification, record reproducible sanitized evidence, prioritize confirmed risk, and retest the fix.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
